p.title: Who chokes under pressure? The Big Five personality traits and decision-making under pressure

ext.title: Who chokes under pressure (Big Five, decision-making)
ext.venue: Personality and Individual Differences, 74 (2015) 22-28. Texas A&M University. DOI 10.1016/j.paid.2014.10.009 (from the text's header).
ext.document_type: Journal article, two-experiment empirical study (lab experiments with undergraduates)
ext.coverage: Full text read in three chunks (lines 0-998), covering title, abstract, introduction, Experiment 1 method and results, Experiment 2 method and results, general discussion, limitations, references, and Tables 1-5 with notes. No Paul markup files existed (the computed task listed "(none)"), so paul_markup is empty. Nothing was skipped. The paper has no content on lobbying, networks, path-finding, allocation, elections, persuasion/turnout, legislators or text measurement.
ext.research_question: Whether the Big Five personality traits predict who thrives or chokes under pressure during dynamic decision-making, i.e., which traits predict performance decrements under social pressure (Exp 1) and under combined social plus time pressure (Exp 2). Neuroticism was the a priori focus; the other four traits were treated as exploratory (Intro, p. 23; Sections 2.2.3 and 4).
ext.theory: Trait activation theory (Tett & Guterman, 2000) plus distraction theory (Lewis & Linder, 1997; Beilock & Carr, 2005; Beilock et al., 2004): pressure consumes working-memory resources; neurotic individuals experience more anxiety and intrusive thoughts, so they are more likely to choose the immediately rewarding option.
ext.data: Experiment 1: N = 127 undergraduates at Texas A&M (76 female, 51 male), course credit. Low-pressure n = 63; high-pressure n = 64 (random assignment, Section 2.1.1). Unit: individual participant, each completing 250 trials. Experiment 2: N = 65 undergraduates (37 female, 28 male), course credit (Section 3.1.1). Three participants were excluded for completion time more than 2 SD from the mean (Section 3.2.1), so the analysed N is about 62. The reported regression df F(5,55) implies N = 61; the paper does not reconcile this. Period: not stated (Psychtoolbox for Matlab v2.5 on PCs).
ext.method: Lab experiments with a dynamic two-option decision task (Gureckis & Love, 2009; Worthy et al., 2011, 2012). The Increasing option pays less immediately but raises both options' future payoffs, so it is optimal. The Decreasing option pays more immediately but lowers future payoffs. Trial-by-trial foregone payoffs are shown. Dependent variable: average proportion of Increasing-option selections over 250 trials. Personality was measured with the 44-item Big Five Inventory. Experiment 1 analysis: Pearson correlations within each condition (Table 2); a two-step hierarchical regression (Step 1: condition dummy and five traits; Step 2: condition x trait interactions), then separate regressions within each condition to locate the interaction (Section 2.2.3; Table 3). Balance check: t-tests on the five traits by condition, Bonferroni-corrected, none significant at p > .01 (Section 2.2.1). Experiment 2: same task plus a 1705 s time limit with live On Pace / Behind Pace feedback; correlations with completion time and performance (Table 4) and a multiple regression of the five traits on performance (Table 5). There was no low-pressure arm in Experiment 2.
ext.identification: Experiment 1 identifies the pressure effect by random assignment to pressure condition (social pressure: a fictitious partner and an $8 shared bonus contingent on reaching 16,000 points). Personality is measured, not manipulated, so trait effects are associations, not causal effects. Experiment 2 has no concurrent control: it is compared to the Experiment 1 control sample (Section 3.3, p. 26), and combines social and time pressure, so its trait effects are not randomized. The authors frame Experiment 2 as a replication test of the Experiment 1 neuroticism effect.
ext.scope: Population: undergraduates at one US university (Texas A&M), recruited for course credit. Era: 2014 data collection (exact dates not stated). Institution: university laboratory. Domain: individual (not group) decision-making in one laboratory task. The authors say results may be limited to the decision-making domain and may not extend to other high-pressure situations (Section 4.1).

key_findings.finding: Exp 1 condition x neuroticism interaction: neuroticism had no significant relation to performance in the low-pressure condition but negatively predicted performance under social pressure.
key_findings.numbers: Interaction DR2 = .06, F(11,115) = 1.96, p = .04; condition x N b = .45, p = .02; high-pressure N b = .50, p < .01; low-pressure N not significant.

key_findings.finding: Exp 1 main effects: pressure lowered performance; neuroticism negatively predicted performance in the first-step model. The first-step model only approached significance.
key_findings.numbers: Step 1 R2 = .10, F(6,120) = 2.14, p = .054; condition b = .43, p = .02; neuroticism b = .25, p = .01; conscientiousness b = .16, p = .09 (trend).

key_findings.finding: Exp 1 correlations within condition: no trait correlated significantly with performance in the low-pressure condition; under pressure, conscientiousness and neuroticism were negatively correlated with performance. The conscientiousness link did not survive the regression and was not replicated in Exp 2.
key_findings.numbers: High pressure: C r = .27, p < .05; N r = .34, p < .01. Low pressure: none significant.

key_findings.finding: Exp 1 agreeableness interaction was a non-significant trend. Higher agreeableness was associated with lower performance under pressure, but not significantly.
key_findings.numbers: Condition x A b = .33, p = .08 (trend); high-pressure A b = .18, p = .17 (ns).

key_findings.finding: Exp 2 (social plus time pressure) replicated the neuroticism effect. Neuroticism and agreeableness both negatively predicted performance; the overall model was significant. Conscientiousness did not predict performance under time pressure.
key_findings.numbers: Model R2 = .19, F(5,55) = 2.61, p < .05; N b = .31, p < .05; A b = .36, p < .01; O, C and E not significant (Table 5 reports b = .16, .16, .06 without significance marks).

key_findings.finding: Exp 2 correlations: agreeableness negatively correlated with performance; neuroticism and conscientiousness were negative but non-significant; completion time correlated strongly with performance.
key_findings.numbers: A r = .29, p < .05; N r = .16 (ns); C r = .16 (ns); completion time x performance r = .62, p < .01.

key_findings.finding: Exp 1 post-task importance ratings did not differ significantly by condition; the low-pressure group rated performance importance slightly lower.
key_findings.numbers: Low M = 4.68 (SD 2.42); high M = 5.17 (SD 2.14); not significant.

key_findings.finding: Authors' overall conclusion: neuroticism is consistently linked to choking under pressure in this task; agreeableness is an unexpected exploratory finding; the conscientiousness result is not supported.
key_findings.numbers: No new numbers; summarizes the above.

measures: Big Five Inventory (BFI), 44 items, 5-point Likert (John, Donahue & Kentle, 1991). Cronbach's alpha .79-.88 (M = .83); convergent r = .73 with NEO-FFI and r = .81 with TDA (Section 2.1.2.1).
Decision-making performance: average proportion of Increasing-option selections across 250 trials (dependent variable in both experiments).

Pressure manipulation: social pressure via a fictitious partner and an $8 bonus contingent on reaching 16,000 points (about 80% optimal choices). Experiment 2 adds time pressure (1705 s limit, live On Pace / Behind Pace feedback).
Post-task importance rating on a 1 (not at all) to 7 (extremely) scale (Section 2.1.3).
limitations: Social pressure included a monetary incentive absent from the low-pressure arm, so monetary and social pressure are confounded (Section 4.1).
Neuroticism group means differed between Experiment 1 conditions (low-pressure higher); the authors say this could have skewed results (Section 4.1).
No pressure manipulation check, anxiety or mood measure, or working-memory capacity measure; the working-memory mechanism is inferred, not tested (Section 4.1).
Between-subjects design with no within-subject control of group differences (Section 4.1).
Self-reported pressure did not differ significantly between conditions, and the low-pressure mean was higher than in earlier studies (Section 2.2.1, footnote 1).
Experiment 2 has no concurrent control; it is compared to the Experiment 1 control sample (Section 3.3).
The conscientiousness effect appeared in Experiment 1 correlations but not in the regression, and did not replicate in Experiment 2 (Sections 3.3 and 4).
The agreeableness finding is unanticipated and labelled exploratory (Section 4); its Experiment 1 interaction was not significant.
Sample: undergraduates at one university, individual decisions only; generalization limited (Section 4.1).

Reporting inconsistencies: Experiment 2 mean completion time is 1699 s in the text but 1670 s (SD 55.73) in Table 4; the text's 2 SD cutoff of 292 s does not match Table 4's SD. The Experiment 2 regression df F(5,55) implies N = 61, not the about 62 implied by excluding 3 of 65.
Footnote 2: the 1705 s limit required responses about 25% faster (about 500 ms per trial) than the Experiment 1 average of about 680 ms (Section 3.1, footnote 2).
references_of_note: Worthy, Otto & Maddox (2012), Working-memory load and temporal myopia in dynamic decision-making, J. Exp. Psych: LMC. Shows WM load shifts this exact task toward immediate rewards; the closest building block for the WM mechanism.

Beilock & Carr (2005), When high-powered people fail: working memory and choking under pressure in math, Psychological Science. Source of the social-pressure manipulation and the WM-distraction account.
Beilock, Kulp, Holt & Carr (2004), More on the fragility of performance, J. Exp. Psych: General. Pressure-induced WM distraction.
DeCaro, Thomas, Albert & Beilock (2011), Choking under pressure: multiple routes to skill failure, J. Exp. Psych: General. Pressure enhances WM distraction in the same social-pressure paradigm.
Tett & Guterman (2000), trait activation theory, J. Research in Personality. Theoretical basis for the trait-by-situation prediction.
Gureckis & Love (2009), Learning in noise: dynamic decision-making in a variable environment, J. Mathematical Psychology. Source of the decision task.
Worthy, Markman & Maddox (2009), Choking and excelling under pressure in experienced classifiers, Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics. Earlier social-pressure work.

short_quotes.quote: Neuroticism negatively predicted performance under social pressure

rel.summary_md:
Byrne, Silasi-Mansat and Worthy ran two lab experiments with Texas A&M undergraduates. Experiment 1 had N = 127, randomised to low or high social pressure. Experiment 2 had about 61 to 62 analysed, under social plus time pressure, with no control arm. The task was a dynamic two-choice task in which picking the option that pays less now but more later is optimal. Big Five traits came from the self-report BFI. Neuroticism was the pre-specified trait, and it was the only effect that held in both experiments. In Experiment 1 it had no effect at low pressure but predicted worse performance under pressure: condition x N b = .45, p = .02; added R2 for the interaction step = .06. Experiment 2 repeated it (N b = .31, p < .05). Agreeableness was exploratory. Its Experiment 1 interaction was only a trend (p = .08); it was significant only in the uncontrolled Experiment 2 (b = .36, p < .01). The conscientiousness correlation (r = .27 under pressure) did not survive regression and did not replicate. Extraversion was null. The paper itself flags that money and social pressure are confounded, that there was no manipulation check, and that the working-memory mechanism was never measured.

Why it matters here: this is the citation behind the receptivity layer's susceptibility composite (`.40A + .30N - .20C - .10E`). It reads that composite as how much a legislator moves under lobbying pressure. The paper only partly supports that. Its outcome is worse choices on a delayed-reward task, not giving in to persuasion. Its sample is students, not legislators. Its strongest trait (N) gets a smaller weight than its weakest positive trait (A). The project's own well-powered test of Byrne's mechanism came back null: H5, N x loss domain, partial r = +0.036, n = 441. So the N slot is cited to theory with no validation behind it, and should keep the UNVERIFIED label.

bearings.paper_claim: Neuroticism is the only trait that predicted worse performance under pressure in both experiments. Exp 1: condition x N b = .45, p = .02 (sign as given in the extract; the text says a negative effect); added R2 for the interaction step = .06, F(11,115) = 1.96, p = .04; under high pressure N b = .50, p < .01; under low pressure, ns. Exp 2 (social plus time pressure): N b = .31, p < .05; model R2 = .19. Agreeableness: the Exp 1 interaction was only a trend (b = .33, p = .08); significant only in Exp 2, which had no control arm (b = .36, p < .01). The authors call A 'exploratory'.
bearings.system_side: The susceptibility composite weights A at .40 and N at .30 ('A ranked above N per the user's framing'). The docstring says high A adds to N-driven choking 'under social pressure (their Exp-2 interaction)'. Exp 2 has no low-pressure arm, so it cannot show an interaction: the A result is a main effect in one uncontrolled sample. The default behavioural basis fills the A slot with cooperation_v2 (cross-party cosponsorship share, rho .888 with bpf), not trait agreeableness. susc drives susc_mult [0.70, 1.30] and edge_mult [0.80, 1.20], and through pressure_mult it feeds the flip, LT and cascade engines.
bearings.code_ref: fec/members/receptivity_layer.py:6-14 (docstring attribution), :186 (behavioural composite .40*coop+.30*Nn-.20*dil-.10*dom), :189 (lexical composite .40*A+.30*N-.20*Cc-.10*E), :47 (SUSC_GAINS); fec/moneyball_core.py:202-213 (rc reader)
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak transfer. (1) Construct: the paper's outcome is choosing a smaller-now reward over the better long-run option on a lab task, not being moved by an outside persuader. A 'choker' makes worse choices; that does not make them more persuadable. (2) Population: undergraduates earning course credit at one university, individual decisions, an $8 bonus. Not elected legislators facing lobbyists. (3) Measurement: the paper uses the self-report BFI. The system uses text or behavioural proxies: affective_n, and cooperation_v2 for A. (4) Size: trait effects explain about 6% of variance in the lab, with no anchor for the ±30% multiplier range. The paper supports the direction of an N-under-pressure term. It does not support A outweighing N, and does not support the size of the term.

bearings.paper_claim: Under high pressure, conscientiousness correlated negatively with performance (C r = .27, p < .05; the text reports a negative association). It fell to a trend in regression (b = .16, p = .09) and did not replicate in Exp 2 (r = .16 ns; b ns). Extraversion was null in both experiments.
bearings.paper_location: Section 2.2.2, Table 2; Section 2.2.3, Table 3; Section 3.3; Section 4
bearings.system_side: The composite subtracts .20*C (diligence in the behavioural basis) and .10*E (dominance), so high-C and high-E members count as less susceptible. The docstring already says these dampeners are 'OUR design priors, NOT Byrne findings', and that the paper's C signal was 'opposite-signed'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The only C evidence in the paper points the other way: higher C, worse under pressure. It is weak and unreplicated. The citation is honest in the docstring, but the composite is still labelled 'Byrne et al. choking composite' at :189. This bearing only says the C and E terms carry no support from this paper, so the provenance string at :233 ('Byrne2015 choking (susc)') overstates what the paper backs.

bearings.paper_claim: The paper explains N-driven choking by working memory: pressure and anxiety use up working memory, so neurotic people take the immediate reward. The authors say they measured no anxiety, mood or working-memory capacity, and ran no pressure manipulation check. Self-rated importance did not differ by condition (Low M = 4.68 vs High M = 5.17, ns), so the mechanism is inferred, not measured.
bearings.system_side: affective_n (LIWC i + negemo - posemo, plus LLM pessimism/anxiety/depression/volatility, residualized on E and party) fills the N slot that receptivity_layer labels as Byrne's channel. The component's own question asks whether affective N predicts yielding under pressure. The project already ran that test as H5 (pinkN x loss-domain on Nokken-Poole drift, n = 441, one look): partial r = +0.036, NULL. Genre transfer also failed (rho .050 / .161).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Byrne gives a theoretical reason to keep an N slot. It gives no evidence that text-measured affective content in interviews is the anxiety-under-pressure facet the paper invokes. The project's own audit notes affective-content N 'does not converge with comfort-curve (different N-facet ... vs reactivity-under-pressure)'. Even the source study did not measure its mechanism, so a null in legislators does not contradict Byrne, and Byrne does not rescue the null. The N contribution should keep its UNVERIFIED label (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: The agreeableness result rests on self-report BFI agreeableness predicting worse task performance. It is exploratory and significant only in the uncontrolled Exp 2 (b = .36, p < .01). The paper has nothing on projected or communal rhetoric.
bearings.system_side: The persona channel reads warm or communal rhetoric as 'approachable-agreeable (Byrne susceptible)'. It blends persona_susc_z = .60 z(communion) - .40 z(agency) into susceptibility at PERSONA_W 0.30 (kept by owner ruling).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Byrne's claim is about self-reported trait A, and only weakly. It says nothing about how communal a member's public rhetoric sounds. Citing Byrne for the persona's susceptibility direction is a second hop the paper does not cover. PERSONA_W is owner policy; this is a provenance note, not a removal proposal.

gaps_exposed: The paper's construct is worse decisions under pressure, not being moved by a persuader. The system has no evidence connecting the two. The prospective H2 contract (Spearman of pressure_mult vs |tier movement|) is still the only planned test, and F5 found it underpowered (72 of 511 new-event members).

No anxiety or stress-state measure exists for members at the time they are lobbied. Byrne's effect appears only under pressure. The system applies trait N to every member all the time; the loss-domain flag is the only situational switch, and H5 found no N x loss interaction.

The ±30% susc_mult range and the .40/.30/.20/.10 weights have no anchor in effect sizes. The paper's trait effects are small (added R2 = .06; model R2 .10 to .19), and the ordering is set by owner framing, not evidence.

The paper's single replicated finding is N. The system's default behavioural basis puts its largest weight (.40) on cooperation_v2, which nearly duplicates bpf (rho .888). bpf already enters the targeting product, so the slot that carries the most weight has the least Byrne support.
flags: Citation mislabel at fec/members/receptivity_layer.py:7-8. The docstring calls the agreeableness effect 'their Exp-2 interaction'. Exp 2 had no low-pressure arm, so no interaction could be tested. The only A interaction was in Exp 1, and it was a non-significant trend (p = .08).

Ordering conflict. The paper's evidence ranks N (pre-specified, replicated) above A (exploratory, uncontrolled). The composite weights A .40 above N .30 on owner framing. That is a legitimate owner choice, but the Byrne label at :189 and the provenance string at :233 suggest the paper backs it.

N-slot status: the project's Byrne-mechanism test (H5, n = 441) was NULL, and genre transfer failed. Any statement that receptivity 'implements Byrne' must carry the UNVERIFIED label (DE-062), and must not be described as validated susceptibility.

Coefficient signs in the extracted paper text are printed without minus signs (for example 'N b = .25'). Direction here is taken from the authors' prose ('negatively predicted'). Check against the PDF before quoting a sign.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul did not annotate this paper. His position on the receptivity layer is that psychological traits should adjust how a member responds to pressure, as edge parameters. Byrne agrees with that idea in principle: a trait-by-situation interaction exists for N. It disagrees on three specifics. First, the paper's outcome is choking, meaning worse decisions on a delayed-reward task, not being persuaded. Second, Paul's framing that very agreeable or submissive members should be 'very susceptible' rests on Byrne's weakest result (exploratory, uncontrolled), not its strongest. Third, the C and E dampeners are not Byrne findings, and the C evidence runs the opposite way. His notes are stale against the system in the way already recorded: the H5 Nokken-drift look tested exactly Byrne's N-under-pressure mechanism and came back null. The layer now runs on behavioural and affective proxies, not Big Five traits.

related.why: It supplies the loss-domain pt_mult in the same receptivity layer. The H5 test crossed Byrne's N with Linde-Vis's loss domain and found no interaction. Both papers test elite or student decisions under pressure, and both find that effects in elites are smaller or unproven.

A systematic review of how traits change the effect of persuasion strategies. That is the persuadability construct the receptivity layer actually needs, which Byrne's choking-on-a-task design does not measure.
It is the incent_mult term multiplied into the same pressure_mult product as Byrne's susceptibility term. Both are cited at receptivity_layer.py:6-21.

Expert ratings of US senators' traits, including N, are the gold panel that could test whether the system's N-slot measure is neuroticism at all. Byrne's mechanism depends on that before it can transfer.
A text-based emotional-stability measure. It bears on whether affective-content N from speech captures the anxiety facet Byrne's mechanism relies on.
The lexical Big Five basis (RECEPT_TRAITS=lexical) that fills Byrne's composite at receptivity_layer.py:189 comes from Ramey-style speech measures. Byrne used the self-report BFI.
